140	
141	# Applications: True Cost of Tommy John Surgery (SSAC19)
142	
143	## Where this applies
144	
145	- Inference: Treat output metrics as unreliable when fatigue is present. McNally's group found that pitch velocity dipped around inning five while elbow stress rose instead of falling, so the velocity-stress link broke down in fatigued pitchers [05:40]. At Baylor the analogous check is whether a performance output (sprint speed, jump height) holds while a driver or strategy metric changes late in a session or week.
146	- Inference: Quantify availability lost per injury type with Athletic Medicine. The talk counted about 200 surgeries and 180 days missed of the MLB calendar on average [12:14]. A Baylor version counts games and practices missed by injury type and position group, with no salary figure.
147	- Inference: Add prior surgery or overuse history to recruiting medical grading questions with Athletic Medicine. The talk cites a Mayo study finding up to 10% of drafted pitchers had already had the surgery [08:11], which suggests earlier overuse history changes what a prospect brings.
148	- Inference: Borrow the decision-tree format for return-to-play conversations (try conservative care or choose surgery) as an illustration for coaches. The talk's model compared expected wins above replacement for two paths and showed where each wins on a sensitivity grid [16:47], [17:19]. It is a communication tool, not a clinical rule.
149	
150	## Eric's baseline
151	
152	- Eric's baseline: Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through load progression and collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, course team position). McNally likewise says we are good at prevention but cannot curb these injuries [03:39]. Agrees.
153	- Eric's baseline: Abrupt changes in volume or intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, course team position). McNally points to year-round, early specialization with no rest as the second cause [06:40]. Extends, with a youth-sport mechanism the baseline does not cover.
154	- Eric's baseline: Bodyweight-control competency comes before loaded work (Inferred, course team position). McNally advises core and bodyweight exercises such as planks over heavy lifting for a 13-year-old [24:11]. Agrees.
155	- Eric's baseline: Force-plate reporting picks output, driver and strategy metrics (adopted from Hawkin Dynamics, not Eric's own framework). The fatigue finding [05:40] is an example where output alone misleads. Extends.
156	- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine decisions on return to performance and is not stated as the decision-maker (Explicit, Playbook p.6). The talk says its model does not replace clinical decision-making [16:47]. Agrees. The baseline holds no specific return-to-play criteria, so the talk adds nothing to compare against.
157	
158	## What would have to be true
159	
160	- Injury history and missed-time records kept consistently by Athletic Medicine, at a sample size large enough to compare by position group.
161	- For any decision model, real inputs: healing likelihood by path, expected performance after return, and timing in the season. The talk says these inputs drive the answer [16:16].
162	- For wearable stress findings, a device and protocol that fit the Baylor sport; the talk's sleeve relies on a throwing motion and cannot measure hitters [21:23].
163	
164	## Do not apply when
165	
166	- The sport is not baseball pitching. The talk says this injury is essentially one position of one sport [21:54]. Do not read across to football injuries.
167	- Salary-based cost figures. Baylor athletes have no player salaries; half a billion dollars over 2004 to 2014 [12:44] and dollars per WAR [10:43] do not transfer to college.
168	- You need effect estimates. The decision-model example (1.6 versus 1.3 expected wins above replacement [16:47]) is a single sample case with chosen inputs. The cohort of 150 had an uncontrolled second analysis [18:19], and the salary study was under review [11:44].
169	- Clinical decisions. The speaker says the model does not replace clinical judgement [16:47].
170	
171	## First step
172	
173	List the three or four output metrics Applied Performance already reports from a daily or weekly session, and write next to each the driver or strategy metric that would show a fatigue-related change. This is a planning list only and changes no process.

45	A research-paper-competition talk that relates inertial sensor training load to non-contact time-loss injuries in football. It starts with the limits of earlier load and injury papers (binary injury coding, no censoring, small samples, thresholds that vary by team, retrospective rather than predictive) and cites work finding single-club models predict poorly on unseen data. The study followed 101 players for one season with 29 non-contact injuries. The best model combined total player load, low player load and high impacts: higher volume and higher physical intensity went with higher risk, and the speaker frames this as risk context for practitioners, not prediction.
46	
47	## Key claims
48	
49	- Non-contact injuries matter because they are thought to be partly due to training errors: too much too soon, too much for too long, or too little [03:03].
50	- Earlier papers often merge contact and non-contact injuries, mix time loss and non-time loss, skip censoring, give thresholds that differ across papers, and are retrospective [03:33], [04:04], [05:06], [06:08].
51	- A cited Australian football study found single-club injury models predicted poorly on unseen data [06:39], [07:10].
52	- The aim was to find associations between training load variables and non-contact time-loss injury, not to predict before a session [07:41].
53	- Metrics used were total player load, four player load effort bands, impacts (three thresholds) and IMA (three thresholds) [08:12], [08:42], [09:12].
54	- The speaker argues IMA helps with linemen because GPS-type measures are less reliable for high-intensity work in spaces under 20 meters [09:44].
55	- The joint model (total player load, player load low, impacts high) fit best; total player load and impacts high carried the highest added risk, and player load low was inversely related [14:20], [14:51], [15:22].
56	- Position group did not add explanatory value, possibly because of too few injuries per group [15:22], [15:53].
57	- Volume and intensity are risk factors to be combined with coaches' own judgment [15:53], [16:23].
58	- Injury is multifactorial; intrinsic and extrinsic factors and their change over a season would be needed for prediction [17:24], [17:54].
59	
60	## Numbers and definitions
61	
62	- Hundreds of millions: about 200 million dollars per year paid to players on injured reserve, in "some articles" [01:02].
63	- Knee injuries 3.1 per 1000 athlete exposures; hip and hamstring 2.2 per 1000 (ten years of NFL training camp data, cited work by "feely and colleagues", caption spelling) [02:03].
64	- Athlete exposure: one athlete in one game or training session [02:33].
65	- Season length: 16 NFL games, 9 to 13 in college [01:32].
66	- Sample: 101 football athletes, one full season preseason through regular season [11:14].
67	- Definition: non-contact injury that caused missed later sessions or games, coded by a medical professional [11:14], [11:45].
68	- Training load normalized per minute and standardized by position group [11:45], [12:15].
69	- Models: logistic regression, compared with Bayesian information criterion and out-of-sample likelihood, with leave-one-out-style cross validation [12:47], [13:18]. Caption reads "four logistic regression models" as "for"; model count is ambiguous (one per variable group plus a joint model).
70	- 29 non-contact injuries [13:18].
71	- Caption problems: the figure "200 million dollars" at [01:02] appears as captioned; "Bayesian information criterion" is clear; effect sizes (odds ratios) are not given.

74	
75	- Catapult-type inertial sensors with player load, effort bands, impacts and IMA (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer) [08:12], [09:12].

100	# Applications: Volume and Intensity in Injury Incidence in Football Athletes
101	
102	## Where this applies
103	
104	- Inference: Catapult practice reporting. The talk's three useful metrics (total player load as volume, impacts high as intensity, player load low as protective) [14:51], [15:22] suggest which columns to review beside the standard load view after each practice, rather than relying on one load number.
105	- Inference: Line play monitoring. The speaker argues IMA is more informative for linemen than GPS-style distance because of small-space, high-intensity work [09:44]. This applies to how Eric reports OL and DL sessions, where total distance may under-describe load.
106	- Inference: Injury logging. The talk's definition (non-contact, time loss, medically coded, athlete removed from the injury day's data after the event [11:14], [12:15]) can be used as a template for how Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance code injuries so load analyses are comparable.
107	- Inference: Preseason camp planning. Q&A says most injuries happened in training camp [22:05], so camp-week load comparisons by position group are where to look first.
108	
109	## Eric's baseline
110	
111	- Eric's baseline: The core GPS metrics tracked include player load, field time and IMA for indoor sessions, in the Catapult workflow. The talk uses the same families of metrics, so it agrees with the tracked set but extends it with injury analysis.
112	- Eric's baseline: No sport- or position-specific GPS thresholds exist in the data dictionary, and no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric. The talk extends this: it shows how a team might build position-standardized load measures (z-type scaling within position [11:45]) but gives no thresholds, and the speaker warns published thresholds vary by team [05:06].
113	- Eric's baseline: Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, and abrupt progression is treated as a driver (Inferred, course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The speaker's stance that the aim is associated risk, not prediction [07:41], agrees.
114	- Eric's baseline: "Culture of fear" criticism of load monitoring (Inferred, course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk's cautious framing, a risk factor that a coach combines with experience [16:23], is compatible.
115	
116	## What would have to be true
117	
118	- Enough non-contact time-loss injuries to model. The talk had 29 injuries across 101 athletes in one season [13:18], and still could not model position groups [15:22].
119	- Clean, consistent injury coding by Athletic Medicine and a rule for censoring athletes who leave a session injured [12:47].
120	- Same device settings and band thresholds across the season; the speaker says the effort bands and IMA each use fixed thresholds [08:42], [09:12] but does not give their values.
121	- Game load, which the talk lacked [16:53]; Baylor game data would need to be added to say anything about game injuries.
122	- Out-of-sample checking, since the speaker cites work showing single-club models predict poorly on unseen data [06:39].
123	
124	## Do not apply when
125	
126	- Using these results as thresholds for Baylor athletes. One team, one season and 29 injuries cannot support a cut point, and the speaker himself says thresholds bounce around [05:06].
127	- Using it to change practice plans because a session scored high on impacts. The result is an association, not a predictive tool [07:41].
128	- Applying to non-football athletes or to games.
129	- Reading it as evidence for a mobility screen: the speaker says no research links specific joint range or posture to injury [20:29].
130	
131	## First step
132	
133	Export one season of Baylor Catapult data to a spreadsheet with total player load per minute and IMA counts by position group, and match it to the Athletic Medicine non-contact time-loss injury list. Just describe it; build no model.

## Summary

The speaker, a sports medicine physician and endocrinologist who co-founded a women's health and sports performance institute, argues that research on female athletes is thin and often poorly built. She gives the history of excluding women from research, the health burdens female athletes face, and the results of literature audits that score studies on population, athlete caliber, menstrual status method, journal and sample size. She warns about unvalidated wearables, weak hormone measurement, survey bias and AI repeating errors, and offers a workflow for validating wearable data. Her answer to closing the gap is teamwork across clinicians, athletes and data analysts.

23	## Summary
24	
25	The speaker, a sports medicine physician and endocrinologist who co-founded a women's health and sports performance institute, argues that research on female athletes is thin and often poorly built. She gives the history of excluding women from research, the health burdens female athletes face, and the results of literature audits that score studies on population, athlete caliber, menstrual status method, journal and sample size. She warns about unvalidated wearables, weak hormone measurement, survey bias and AI repeating errors, and offers a workflow for validating wearable data. Her answer to closing the gap is teamwork across clinicians, athletes and data analysts.
26	
27	## Key claims
28	
29	- Women's sport is growing: Title IX, women now have 44% of sport opportunities, more than 160 female sports leagues exist, and fandom has risen, but gaps remain in media investment and prize money. [03:06] [03:35] [04:07] [06:40]
30	- Female athletes face higher rates of concussion, ACL tears and bone stress injuries, and relative energy deficiency in sport is very prevalent, partly through inadvertent under-fueling. [06:40] [07:10]

The speaker says asking is not the same as testing, and that a withdrawal bleed is not a natural cycle [16:25]. Any internal analysis that groups athletes by cycle phase needs that field first.

Inference: Applying her audit fields to the Zotero library for any women's-sport question: population, athlete caliber tier, menstrual status method, research theme, journal, sample size [15:23][16:56]. # Evidence Stacking: Don't Decide on One Dramatic Signal

**What it is** — Weber's central question for any consequential decision, per the lesson summary: does staff have enough independent, relevant information to act (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). A dramatic single result or first impression should prompt further investigation, not settle the decision. An evidence stack combines the event/problem history, clinical findings where relevant, the athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance under the conditions the decision actually concerns (00:00–02:20). His practical takeaway: define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that each add distinct evidence rather than repeating what is already known (17:35–18:15). This is the same caution Weber repeats in narrower form elsewhere in the course: in Lab 2A, one test returning to baseline is treated as one data point rather than a stand-alone clearance (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02); in Webinar 1 Part III, one favorable test result is not a complete return-to-running answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); and in Podcast 1, he warns specifically against treating a single red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24).

**Why it works** — Weber's own stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to separate meaningful change from noise and to communicate decisions with appropriate confidence (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). **Inference:** the likely reason combining sources helps is that different evidence types fail in different, largely independent ways: a single clinical impression, a single hop-test result, and a single speed-exposure metric can each individually mislead, but they are unlikely to all mislead in the same direction at once. Updating the working assessment as each new piece arrives, illustrated with Weber's soccer-knee and hamstring anecdotes (02:20–17:35), is more robust than treating any one piece as decisive.

**When to apply** — Any return-to-play, load, or selection decision where one metric alone is being used to justify the call, especially under time pressure or when a result is unusually dramatic (very good or very bad). **Eric's baseline:** the course transcripts in Eric's own corpus argue "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. But you do have to have a good coach's eye," while Eric's own SportSmith writing moved the opposite direction on daily monitoring by replacing subjective wellness surveys with objective mRSI [method-baseline.md Tensions #3]. **Inference:** evidence stacking offers a synthesis rather than forcing a choice between those two positions: the coach's eye is one more independent stream to stack alongside the objective metric, not a competitor to it.

**When NOT to apply** — Per the lesson summary's own caveat (not Weber's words), the anecdotes illustrate a reasoning approach and do not establish that a triple-hop baseline can diagnose a knee injury; medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions (Podcast 2 summary, practical takeaway). It also does not specify how many independent streams are enough for a given decision; that judgment is left to the practitioner.

**Example** — Weber's hamstring case: clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at matched speeds, specifically to close the gap between controlled tests and actual field demands before returning the athlete to competition (Podcast 2 summary, 10:30–17:35). The reported outcome is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule. Untested anecdote (n=1). The mechanics comparison used SpeedSig, Weber's own product (Podcast 2 transcript 00:15:52 to 00:16:18); treat the case as an illustration by an interested party, not evidence for the product or the return pathway.

# Many MLB Pitchers Do Not Return to Prior Durability After UCL Reconstruction

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally (sports medicine orthopedic surgeon and Detroit Lions team physician, per the host, z_6M5r7031A [00:00]) reports public-data cohort results on ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) reconstruction, "Tommy John surgery," in Major League Baseball pitchers. The speaker says he was told early on that the surgery "works for everybody" (z_6M5r7031A [09:13]).
- **Cohort:** 150 MLB pitchers who had the surgery, of whom 140 were "established," defined as pitching in 10 or more games in a season (z_6M5r7031A [09:13]).
- **Not back:** 20% of the established pitchers never pitched in the majors again (z_6M5r7031A [09:13] to [09:43]).
- **Back, but reduced:** "one out of three" came back but never reached 10 games a year again, pitching one or two games (z_6M5r7031A [09:43]). The caption does not say whether the denominator is all 140 or only those who returned.
- **Those who returned:** a statistically significant decline in "numerous pitching metrics" (z_6M5r7031A [09:43] to [10:13]). The metrics and effect sizes are not named or shown.
- **Value curve:** wins above replacement (WAR) fell over the 3 years before surgery and took 3 years after return to reach the pre-surgery level. With 12 to 18 months to get back to the majors, he puts the full path at about four to four and a half years (z_6M5r7031A [10:13] to [10:43]).
- **Controls:** in Q&A he says the first data set used age-matched controls and the second was not controlled for starter versus reliever (z_6M5r7031A [18:19]). On recovery by age, the numbers were too small to separate, and the pattern looked like the natural trend with age (z_6M5r7031A [18:50]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for the post-surgery decline. He does say professional tears are usually attritional, a slow wearing down with pathology building up in the elbow (z_6M5r7031A [26:13]). Inference: a WAR decline that starts three years before surgery fits that account, but the talk does not link the two.

**When to apply** — As a reality check on the idea that reconstruction restores a pitcher to prior form, and as an outside comparison when explaining return-to-play expectations for a throwing athlete. # Faster Pitches Put More Stress on the Elbow, Youth and Professional

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally's group at Henry Ford uses a wearable sleeve that detects stress and torque at the medial elbow, "right where the UCL is" (z_6M5r7031A [04:09]). He reports that, "study after study," the faster the pitch, the more elbow stress, and that this is pitch speed, not arm speed (z_6M5r7031A [04:39]). He says it holds for a 12-year-old youth pitcher and for a professional, and that it has been borne out in "numerous" independent studies from his group (z_6M5r7031A [04:39] to [05:10]). He contrasts it with older advice to avoid curveballs and off-speed pitches and "stick with straight fastballs" (z_6M5r7031A [04:39]).

Related statements from the talk:
- Arm slot: studies of slot and release point exist, and "so far" slot has not shown increased elbow stress; this is the group's next stage (z_6M5r7031A [22:33]).
- Device limit: the sleeve relies on a throwing motion, so it cannot measure elbow stress in hitters (z_6M5r7031A [21:23]).
- Trend: average fastball velocity is climbing year over year, which he offers as one of two reasons the injury persists (z_6M5r7031A [04:09]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism. Inference: a faster release plausibly needs more force through the arm, so more load at the elbow is plausible, but the talk does not say so.

**When to apply** — As background when a throwing sport (baseball, softball) asks whether to monitor throwing stress or velocity. Eric's baseline: a test or technology that "doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need" has no place (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3). Inference: ask first what decision a sleeve or velocity number would change, then check validation (the talk does not describe any validation of the sleeve).

**When NOT to apply** — The talk gives no effect sizes, sample sizes or ranges for these studies. The studies are the speaker's group's own, summarized aloud. The sleeve's validity is not discussed in the talk. It covers pitching only; he says UCL injury is essentially one position of one sport (z_6M5r7031A [21:54]). The slot finding is a preliminary "so far." Do not use it as a velocity limit for any athlete.

**Example** — The speaker's own contrast: the old coaching rule was to avoid curveballs and change-ups because of elbow stress, while his group finds high-velocity fastballs also impart greater stress, in a 12-year-old and in a professional (z_6M5r7031A [04:39] to [05:10]).

**Related** — [[claim--fatigue-breaks-the-velocity-elbow-stress-link]] (the same sleeve under fatigue). [[claim--youth-specialization-survey-and-early-surgery]] (the second cause the speaker gives for the injury).

# In Fatigued Pitchers the Velocity-Stress Link Broke Down

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally's group put pitchers through a simulated seven-inning game and asked for a fatigue rating from 1 to 10 after each inning (z_6M5r7031A [05:10]). The ratings rose inning by inning. Peak fastball velocity began to dip around inning five, "not that surprising" to him (z_6M5r7031A [05:10] to [05:40]). What surprised the group: when elbow stress should have come down with the lower velocity, it went up. Compared with pitchers who were not fatigued, "the velocity-stress relationship totally broke down" in fatigued pitchers (z_6M5r7031A [05:40]). The sample size is not stated, and the talk says the study was done "recently."

His hypothesis, offered in Q&A: throwing starts from the toes, back and core, and as those muscles fatigue while the pitcher tries to hold velocity, "the arm's doing everything" (z_6M5r7031A [24:11]). For a 13-year-old's parents he suggests core and bodyweight exercises such as planks, not heavy lifting, and says his group will start looking into this (z_6M5r7031A [24:11] to [24:42]).

**Why it works** — The kinetic-chain account above is the speaker's hypothesis, not a tested result. He illustrates it with his own tennis serve (z_6M5r7031A [23:40] to [24:11]). The simulated-game study did not measure the other body segments in anything the talk reports.

**When to apply** — As a prompt to check whether an output (velocity, jump height, sprint speed) still holds while a driver or strategy metric changes late in a session or week. Eric's baseline: force-plate reporting picks output, driver and strategy metrics (adopted from Hawkin Dynamics, not Eric's own framework; hd-odsf-metrics.md). Inference: this finding is an example of output alone misleading, since the velocity looked acceptable while the stress rose. Eric's baseline: bodyweight-control competency is treated as a marker of injury risk and comes before loaded work (Inferred, HHPR 5355 course team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: this matches the speaker's planks-over-heavy-lifting advice for a young athlete, though the speaker's advice is about a 13-year-old.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one simulated-game study, sample size not stated, no numbers shown for stress or velocity, and the mechanism is a hypothesis. It was pitchers in a simulated game, not a competition. Do not conclude that stress rises with fatigue in other sports or movements. Do not use the kinetic-chain idea to prescribe training; the speaker says he is only starting to study it.

**Example** — The speaker's own: velocity dips at inning five, yet stress rises instead of falling, unlike non-fatigued pitchers (z_6M5r7031A [05:40]).

**Related** — [[claim--faster-pitches-load-the-elbow-more]] (the relationship that broke down).

# Year-Round Youth Baseball: Arm Pain Is Common, Pressure to Play On Is Common

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally gives early single-sport specialization and year-round play as the second reason UCL surgeries are not falling (z_6M5r7031A [06:10] to [07:10]). He says specialization before kids are skeletally mature is "causing a burnout" of muscles and tendons (z_6M5r7031A [07:10]).

- **Survey:** 200 healthy youth baseball players who were not complaining of pain, surveyed "when I was in residency in New York City." 75% admitted arm pain (z_6M5r7031A [07:10]). 25% had symptoms suggestive of a legitimate overuse injury, and 50% felt pressured to play despite admitting arm pain, by coaches and parents (z_6M5r7031A [07:41]).
- **Draft:** a Mayo Clinic study by Chris Camp (caption spelling), which the speaker reports second-hand, found up to 10% of drafted pitchers, high school and college, had already had Tommy John surgery, at an increasing rate year by year (z_6M5r7031A [07:41] to [08:11]).
- **Youngest case:** the youngest he has operated on was 12 (z_6M5r7031A [08:11]).
- **Qualifier (Q&A):** some early throwing is necessary because the arm remodels in childhood, including the humerus, so a child who never threw cannot take up pitching at 12; "the challenge is giving some rest" (z_6M5r7031A [19:51] to [20:21]). Pitch counts are undermined when school and travel leagues each count separately, and 15 warm-up pitches between innings add to a 70-pitch count (z_6M5r7031A [20:21]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated cause is no rest for the shoulder and elbow muscles across fall, winter, spring, summer, travel and high school ball (z_6M5r7031A [06:40]). The survey shows prevalence of pain and perceived pressure; it does not by itself show that specialization caused the injuries. Inference: the survey is cross-sectional, so cause cannot be read from it.

**When to apply** — As an outside prompt when Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance take medical or injury history from incoming baseball or softball athletes. Inference: ask about prior surgery and year-round throwing history, since the draft figure suggests earlier overuse changes what a prospect brings. Eric's baseline: progressions in volume and intensity are kept smooth, and abrupt changes are treated as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, HHPR 5355 course team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: this talk extends that with a youth-sport mechanism, accumulated load with no rest, which the baseline does not cover.

**When NOT to apply** — The survey's sample source, selection method and ages are not given beyond "200 healthy youth baseball players" in one residency setting. Self-reported pain is not a diagnosis. The Mayo figure is "up to 10%" and second-hand. The talk does not show that specialization causes the burnout; that is the speaker's assertion. Baseball pitching only. Not evidence about college or football athletes.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Little League kids icing their elbows after games, and facilities in Michigan full of children playing indoors in snow (z_6M5r7031A [06:10] to [07:10]).

**Related** — [[claim--faster-pitches-load-the-elbow-more]] (the first cause the speaker gives). [[claim--ucl-reconstruction-return-outcomes-mlb-pitchers]] (what happens after surgery).

# Expected Value Decision Analysis for Surgery Versus Non-Operative Care

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally proposes expected value decision analysis as "an adjunct to our clinical care" for a UCL injury, after saying his group has used it in other parts of orthopedic surgery (z_6M5r7031A [15:46], [17:49]). The structure he describes:
1. **Two branches:** surgery, or non-operative treatment (the "top wing" and "bottom wing," z_6M5r7031A [16:16] to [16:47]).
2. **One outcome to maximize:** pitcher wins above replacement (WAR) in his example (z_6M5r7031A [16:47]).

# Before Trying Conservative Care First, Price What Happens If It Fails

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally answers the obvious proposal, "why not just let everybody try non-operative treatment" first, with a question: what if it does not work? (z_6M5r7031A [14:45] to [15:15]). If the trial burns 3 months of rest, activity modification and physical therapy and the athlete still needs surgery, then instead of losing one season by operating at once, "you've now lost two" (z_6M5r7031A [15:15]). His numbers for the two branches: non-operative success of 40 to 80% depending on the case, at most a 3-month downtime (z_6M5r7031A [14:14] to [14:45]); surgery downtime of a year to a year and a half (z_6M5r7031A [14:45]). The follow-on question he poses: "How do we know who can benefit from surgery and who won't?" (z_6M5r7031A [15:15]), which he says is mostly clinical decision-making.

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the season count itself: a failed trial moves the operation later. Inference: because the cost is measured in lost seasons, the timing of the injury within the calendar matters, which fits his own point that spring training and the weeks before the playoffs are different injuries (z_6M5r7031A [16:16]).

**When to apply** — In any conversation where "try rehab first" is proposed for an injury that might still need surgery, to make the failure branch visible to coaches and athletes. Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine on return to performance and is not stated as the decision-maker (Explicit, Playbook p.6). Inference: the heuristic frames the question to ask Athletic Medicine; it does not answer it.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the success ranges are given without sources and the caption for the surgery range is garbled. The speaker's context is one UCL injury in professional pitchers, where a "season" is a fixed competitive calendar. The heuristic says nothing about injuries where conservative care is the standard first step. Not a basis for recommending surgery. The speaker says the choice is clinical.

**Example** — The speaker's own: non-operative treatment tried first fails, and the pitcher "lost two" seasons instead of one (z_6M5r7031A [15:15]).

**Related** — [[framework--expected-value-decision-analysis-for-treatment-choice]] (the model that puts a number on the failure branch).

# About Half a Billion Dollars of MLB Salary Went to UCL Rehab, 2004 to 2014

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]).
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.

**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.

**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Baylor athletes have no player salaries, so dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.

**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).

**Related** — [[claim--ucl-reconstruction-return-outcomes-mlb-pitchers]] (the cohort data that goes with these costs).

# A Checklist for Reading Training-Load and Injury Papers

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") opens his research-competition talk with the limits he sees in the published load and injury literature, from soccer and cricket to rugby and Australian football (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33]). Six checks, each with his stated reason:
1. **Contact versus non-contact.** Some papers code injury as a binary, injured in the session or game or not. Then the reader cannot tell whether load had anything to do with it or whether a player rolled up on another's leg (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33] to [04:04]).
2. **Time loss versus non-time loss.** Without it, severity is unknown. Time-loss injuries are the ones that keep players out (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:04]).
3. **Censoring.** If an athlete is hurt a quarter of the way into a session and removed, and the model does not censor that session, it can produce "really low training loads lead to high amounts of injuries" (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]).
4. **Thresholds.** Papers often end with a "train above X load, Y more injuries" rule, but thresholds "bounce around" between papers, even in one sport, because the samples are small, one team and one to two years of data (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:06]).
5. **Team-specific results.** The speaker says these papers are often less about predicting injury for a sport and more about one team and how its coach prepares it, comparing it to inconsistent coffee-and-wine nutrition headlines (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:37]).
6. **Retrospective versus predictive.** Papers say "prediction" in the title, but the model is never tested on unseen data; they are historical accounts of how injuries took place, which he says is "not necessarily bad" (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:08]).

**Why it works** — Each check is paired with the failure it prevents, as listed above. The speaker gives no evidence on how often each failure occurs in the literature; he describes them as "some of the papers" (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33]). Inference: the checks work as a quick screen because each one changes what the reader can conclude (association versus prediction, one team versus a sport).

**When to apply** — Before acting on a published load-injury result or a vendor claim that load data predicts injury. Eric's baseline: Eric looks at ACWR but does not trust it for anything, calling it "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally," and follows no formal risk model (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: this checklist gives specific reasons for that distrust, such as no unseen-data test and unstable thresholds.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is one researcher's critique, not a validated appraisal tool, and it gives no scoring or cut-off. It is not a replacement for a formal risk-of-bias instrument. It says nothing about the quality of the speaker's own study beyond what he states; see the case-study entry for that.

**Example** — The speaker's own, for check 3: an unadjusted model that kicks out "really low training loads lead to high amounts of injuries" because injured athletes' short sessions are left in (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--single-club-injury-models-predict-poorly-on-unseen-data]] (check 6 in practice). [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (how the speaker's own study handled checks 1 to 3). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. # Single-Club Load Models Predicted Injury Poorly on Unseen Data

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") cites a tweet by Luke Bourne (caption spelling "Luke borne"), a co-author of his paper, saying the sports science industry states "we predict injuries" while the research community says injury prediction is hard and unresolved (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39]). The tweet linked a paper from "David Carey's group out of Australia" (caption spelling). Ward's account of it: the group built predictive models of training load and injury in Australian football, tested them on unseen data, and concluded that models built from a single club's load data showed poor ability to predict injuries on previously unseen data, so they are limited as daily decision tools for practitioners (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39] to [07:10]). No accuracy figures are given in the talk.

Ward adds a contrast: technology companies tell practitioners to "dump your data in" and injury will be predicted, while the people collecting the data know how hard it is to get it clean and coded properly, and injury is multifactorial (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond injury being multifactorial and data quality being hard (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:10]). Inference: a model fit on one club's data may be capturing that club's practices and noise, which would fail on new data, but the talk does not say this.

**When to apply** — As the standard to ask of any vendor or paper claiming prediction: was it tested on unseen data, and at more than one club? Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is followed, and ACWR is looked at but not trusted (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: this is outside support for that decision to avoid formal models.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Ward's secondhand description of one Australian football study, not a first-hand reading of it. The sport (Australian football) and the data source (single club) bound it; the talk does not say it holds for multi-club data or for American football. It is a statement about daily decision tools, not about whether load relates to injury at all; Ward's own study reports associations (see the case-study entry).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the sports science industry says "we predict injuries," the research community says it is hard, and the cited Australian group's out-of-sample test supports the research community (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39] to [07:10]).

**Related** — [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]] (check 6). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[carey-2017-predictive-modelling-of-training-loads-and-injury-in-australian-football]] in the research-paper library; its title matches the paper Ward describes, but this batch did not open it, so verify they are the same study.

# 101 Football Athletes, One Season: Volume and Impacts Tracked Non-Contact Injury

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") and co-authors analyzed one full season, preseason through regular season, in 101 American football athletes (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:14]). The aim was not to predict injuries before a session but to identify the relationship between training-load variables and non-contact time-loss injury, so practitioners get an idea of associated risk (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]).

- **Metrics from inertial sensor units** (vendor not named in the transcript): total player load, four player load effort bands, impacts with three thresholds, and inertial movement analysis (IMA) with three thresholds (TbYgc6_qQzo [08:12] to [09:12]).
- **Injuries:** 29 non-contact time-loss injuries, mostly lower extremity, plus an oblique in a linebacker, a low back strain and an elbow strain in a defensive lineman who was learning a new position (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:18] to [13:49]).
- **Models:** the best model within each metric group, then a joint model. The player load model used total player load and player load "very high"; the IMA and impacts models used all three bands; the joint model used total player load, player load low and impacts high and was "the most useful" for explaining injury (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:49] to [14:20]).
- **Direction of effects:** total player load and impacts high carried the highest increase in risk; player load low had a decreased association (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:20] to [15:22]). Ward reads total player load as volume and impacts high as session intensity or physicality, interesting because collision injuries were not studied (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:51]).
- **Position group:** adding it as a categorical variable did not help in any model, and he suspects too few injuries per group (TbYgc6_qQzo [15:22] to [15:53]).
- **Timing:** in Q&A, most injuries occurred in training camp, very few once the season started (TbYgc6_qQzo [22:05]).
- **Not shown:** effect sizes, thresholds or band values (the transcript gives none), and no game load (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:53]).

**Why it works** — Ward's interpretation for the inverse player-load-low result is that a session cannot be high and low intensity at the same time, so the inverse relation is "logical" (TbYgc6_qQzo [15:22]). The speaker gives no mechanism for why impacts would raise non-contact risk. Inference: it may reflect session physicality or camp-style practice, but the talk does not say.

**When to apply** — As a template for which Catapult-type columns to read beside the standard load view after practice: total volume, a high-intensity impacts count, and the low band, instead of one load number. Eric's baseline: core GPS metrics tracked include player load, field time and IMA for indoor sessions (Explicit, Playbook pp.11-13). Eric's baseline: no sport- or position-specific GPS thresholds exist formally ("They do not exist formally," Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q7). Inference: this study supplies no thresholds to fill that gap. Inference: camp weeks, where most injuries fell here, are where a Baylor descriptive look would start.

**When NOT to apply** — One team, one season, 29 injuries, and no effect sizes. The talk does not name the team or level; a questioner refers to roster reduction to "a final 53" (TbYgc6_qQzo [21:35]), which suggests an NFL-style roster, but that is not confirmed. Association only, with no game load. Injury types were pooled across hamstring, adductor and other injuries (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:23] to [16:53]). Do not set a Baylor load limit from it, and do not change practice plans because one session scored high on impacts. Ward himself says thresholds "bounce around" between studies (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:06]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the defensive lineman's elbow extensor strain came while learning a new position and doing exercises unique to him in training (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (how the data were coded). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. [[claim--ima-informs-linemen-where-gps-distance-does-not]].

# How the Study Coded Injuries, Scaled Load and Censored Sessions

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") describes how his one-season football study handled the limitations he lists in other papers (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]):
1. **Injury definition:** any injury not due to contact with another player that results in the player missing subsequent training sessions or games, "really stringent" so only non-contact time-loss injuries counted (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:14] to [11:45]).
2. **Who coded:** a medical professional present at the diagnoses coded the injuries in a bespoke injury database (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:45]).
3. **Load scaling:** load variables normalized to session minutes (the density of the session), then standardized within each position group, to "borrow some strength" from position-group data because groups have different tasks (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:45] to [12:15]).
4. **Censoring:** an athlete who was injured in a session, evaluated by a medical professional and deemed unable to continue was removed from the data for that injury day, so the shortened session would not pull the data down (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:15] to [12:47]).
5. **Models:** logistic regression models, fit iteratively, with the caption reading "for" (likely "four") separate models for the load-variable groups plus a joint model; the model count is ambiguous in the caption (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:47]). Compared with the Bayesian information criterion and out-of-sample likelihood (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:47] to [13:18]).
6. **Out-of-sample check:** with too little data for a hold-out group, they used "a concept like leave one out cross validation" across the season (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:18]).

**Why it works** — Step 4 answers the problem he names earlier, that without censoring a model can show low loads leading to injuries (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]). Step 1 and 2 answer the contact and severity problem (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33] to [04:04]). The speaker gives no reason for position standardization beyond borrowing strength and position-specific tasks (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:15]).

**When to apply** — As a template for agreeing, between Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance, one injury definition and one rule for sessions where an athlete is injured, before any load analysis. Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-20, NordBord). Inference: consistent injury coding is the same kind of precondition. The speaker's position-group scaling is also the only approach to position-specific load in this batch; Eric's baseline says no sport- or position-specific GPS thresholds exist formally (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q7).

**When NOT to apply** — The out-of-sample check is leave-one-out style within one team's one season, which is not an independent test; the speaker calls it "a concept like" that method. Band thresholds for effort bands and IMA are fixed but their values are not given (TbYgc6_qQzo [08:42] to [09:12]). Position standardization did not produce a position effect with 29 injuries (TbYgc6_qQzo [15:22]). The talk reports no inter-rater check on the injury coding.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a player pulled from a session after a first-quarter-equivalent injury is dropped from that injury day's load data rather than counted with a tiny load (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36], [12:15] to [12:47]).

**Related** — [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]]. [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]].

# Inertial Movement Analysis May Describe Linemen Where GPS Distance Does Not

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") defines inertial movement analysis (IMA) as a count of movements in different directions (forward, backward, right, left and in between), built from accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer data and reported in three threshold bands (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:12]). His argument: GPS-type measures say a lot about outside players such as defensive backs and wide receivers, who produce much locomotor activity, but little about offensive and defensive linemen, because reliability falls when units record high-intensity activity in small spaces, "say below 20 meters," which is what linemen do (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:44]). He says "we think this may be a useful metric" (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:44]).

Support offered, all described verbally without data: earlier work showing the metrics differentiate position groups in running and non-running activity, and proof-of-concept examples: a wide receiver running a straight sprint and a cut, the 5-10-5 pro agility drill, and a sled hit and drive-through (TbYgc6_qQzo [10:14] to [11:14]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the unit-reliability point above. The talk gives no figures for reliability by distance or for how IMA performs for linemen.

**When to apply** — Inference: when reporting offensive and defensive line sessions, where total distance may under-describe the work. Eric's baseline: IMA is among the core GPS metrics tracked, used for indoor sessions without GPS coverage (Explicit, Playbook pp.11-13). Inference: this talk proposes a different use for the same metric, small-space line work, which the baseline does not state.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: no data are shown for the linemen claim, and the examples are single-athlete drills. The 20-meter reliability point is the speaker's statement with no citation. IMA band thresholds are not given. In the injury study, IMA models were fit but the joint model did not retain IMA, and no position-group effect was found, so the study does not show IMA helps for linemen (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:20], [15:22]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a sled hit that the athlete drives through, as an exercise where collisions in small space register differently from running distance (TbYgc6_qQzo [10:44] to [11:14]).

**Related** — [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]] (the study in which IMA was one metric group).

# Inertial Movement Analysis May Describe Linemen Where GPS Distance Does Not

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") defines inertial movement analysis (IMA) as a count of movements in different directions (forward, backward, right, left and in between), built from accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer data and reported in three threshold bands (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:12]). His argument: GPS-type measures say a lot about outside players such as defensive backs and wide receivers, who produce much locomotor activity, but little about offensive and defensive linemen, because reliability falls when units record high-intensity activity in small spaces, "say below 20 meters," which is what linemen do (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:44]). He says "we think this may be a useful metric" (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:44]).

Support offered, all described verbally without data: earlier work showing the metrics differentiate position groups in running and non-running activity, and proof-of-concept examples: a wide receiver running a straight sprint and a cut, the 5-10-5 pro agility drill, and a sled hit and drive-through (TbYgc6_qQzo [10:14] to [11:14]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the unit-reliability point above. The talk gives no figures for reliability by distance or for how IMA performs for linemen.

**When to apply** — Inference: when reporting offensive and defensive line sessions, where total distance may under-describe the work. Eric's baseline: IMA is among the core GPS metrics tracked, used for indoor sessions without GPS coverage (Explicit, Playbook pp.11-13). Inference: this talk proposes a different use for the same metric, small-space line work, which the baseline does not state.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: no data are shown for the linemen claim, and the examples are single-athlete drills. The 20-meter reliability point is the speaker's statement with no citation. IMA band thresholds are not given. In the injury study, IMA models were fit but the joint model did not retain IMA, and no position-group effect was found, so the study does not show IMA helps for linemen (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:20], [15:22]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a sled hit that the athlete drives through, as an exercise where collisions in small space register differently from running distance (TbYgc6_qQzo [10:44] to [11:14]).

**Related** — [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]] (the study in which IMA was one metric group).

# Training Load Gives Risk Context, Not Injury Prediction

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") frames his result as associated risk that practitioners can use "to build appropriate training sessions that are logical and hopefully mitigate injury," not as prediction before a session (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]). He says practitioners can combine volume and intensity findings with the heuristics they have built over years of designing sessions (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:23]). To make a model truly predictive he says it would need much more than load: "we're probably really naive" to think only load factors raise non-contact injury risk; there are intrinsic factors the athlete brings, extrinsic factors of the session, their interactions, and how those interactions change as players adapt or maladapt across a season (TbYgc6_qQzo [17:24] to [17:54]).

Q&A adds two cautions. An audience member argued that training is "endogenous to effort," so correlations could reflect players who try hard in both practice and games, and that random assignment would address it; Ward agreed it would help if a coach would allow it, and noted the group also tracks perceived effort but did not use it in this paper (TbYgc6_qQzo [18:24] to [19:27]). Underreporting of pain by athletes is, he says, one of the most complex limits in collegiate and professional sport (TbYgc6_qQzo [24:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's argument is multifactorial causation, as above. He gives no data that other factors would improve prediction; that is his position, not a result. Inference: treating load as one risk input fits that position and avoids implying a certainty the model lacks.

**When to apply** — When a load report is used in a conversation with coaches about a practice plan. Eric's baseline: the coach's eye flags where to look and data then investigates (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q6). Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through load progression and collaboration with Athletic Medicine (Inferred, HHPR 5355 course team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: both fit Ward's stance that a load measure informs the coach's judgment rather than replacing it.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is the speaker's stance, supported by the limits of his own study (29 injuries, one team, one season) but not tested as a decision approach. It gives no rule for how much weight to give load against other information. The endogeneity concern was raised by an audience member and only partly answered. Eric's baseline: no formal risk model is followed (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: that makes this principle a description of current practice, not a new method for Baylor.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a session scoring high on impacts is a risk factor to weigh against what a coach knows, not a signal to cancel work (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:51], [16:23]).

**Related** — [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]]. [[claim--single-club-injury-models-predict-poorly-on-unseen-data]]. [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]].

# "No Research Links Joint Range or Posture to Injury": Said and Disputed in the Q&A

**What it is** — In Q&A an audience member said a full picture of injury risk needs internal load (heart rate load, time in zone), heart rate variability and recovery profiles, hydration, hip mobility asymmetry and pain and soreness, plus RPE, and that "the number of teams that collect all that data is pretty much zero" (TbYgc6_qQzo [19:59]). Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") answered that his team collects all of it, but disagreed on the hip mobility piece: he said no research has been able to suggest that specific joint ranges of motion or even postures lead to injury or pain, and that you can find correlations in papers that look retrospectively (TbYgc6_qQzo [19:59] to [20:29]). He added that a preseason mobility or posture measure will change as athletes adapt or are given a training intervention, so it would need re-measuring every week, which is possible but hard with about 120 athletes on a collegiate team (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:29] to [20:59]). He agreed the full data would be "really helpful."

Where it is contested: the audience member holds that hip mobility asymmetry belongs in the picture; Ward says no research supports a causal link. The disagreement is inside the talk and is not resolved there.

**Why it works** — Ward's stated reason is that retrospective correlations differ from prediction and that measures taken in preseason go stale as athletes adapt (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:29]). He cites no study for the blanket statement. Inference: "no research has ever" is a strong universal claim made aloud in Q&A and should not be cited as a literature finding.

**When to apply** — As a reason to ask what decision a mobility or posture screen changes before collecting it weekly. Eric's baseline: movement screens are "just collected and referred to for future needs" and change no program decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Eric's baseline: a test that "doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need" has no place (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3). Inference: this exchange supports Eric's own caution about screens, and by his Q3 rule the screens are candidates to retire or to be given a question.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is contested because the talk itself disagrees. Ward's claim is a universal negative with no citation, and the audience member's view was not rebutted with data. Do not cite it as proof that mobility or posture is irrelevant to injury, or as a reason to stop screening in rehab or return-to-play contexts, which the talk does not address. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[afonso-undated-asymmetries-and-injury-risk-when-titles-spin-the-tale]], on asymmetry and injury risk, was not compared in this batch.

**Example** — The speaker's own point: an athlete's hip range measured in preseason and then changed by training means a single preseason value no longer describes him by midseason (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:29]).

**Related** — [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]] (his wider multifactorial view, which includes intrinsic factors).
